78: A wedding Saturday always follows the same script, and you should have it written down before you sell the first date. The hours are indicative and change with the season and the type of event. In the morning, your team finishes the setup of the space: furniture, the ceremony site in the garden, restrooms, lighting and parking. Then the caterer arrives, unloads at the prep and warming kitchen and sets up its area, and a sound check runs with the decibel meter on. In the afternoon the guests arrive and the ceremony takes place; the cocktail hour follows in the garden, the reception in the hall or under the tent and, at the end, the last dance. Load-out starts when the last guest leaves: the caterer removes its equipment and leaves the kitchen clean, and your team breaks down, cleans and closes the parking lot. The split is clear. The venue provides coordination, setup of the space, cleaning, parking and maintenance. The caterer provides the menu, the bar, the servers and its own cooking. That boundary is what frees you from running a kitchen crew and from answering for the food safety of the menu. Direct event costs (cleaning, restroom supplies, generator fuel, parking attendants and security) run about {{coste_directo_pct}} of venue rental and services.
79: Infrastructure is what separates a pretty venue from a venue that works. The case is sized for a hall that seats {{aforo}} guests, but the legal occupant load is set and posted by your fire marshal. ADA-compliant restrooms cost {{inv_aseos}}, with the septic upgrade quoted apart. Parking costs {{inv_parking}}: plan about one space for every 2.5-3 guests. The standby generator ({{inv_generador}}) covers a blackout in the middle of the reception, and the electrical service ({{inv_electrica}}) has to carry the caterer’s kitchen, the sound and the HVAC ({{inv_hvac}}). Sound and a decibel meter ({{inv_sonido}}) are planned from the start, so that the music stays in the hall. Add the caterer’s prep and warming kitchen ({{inv_office}}), where the caterer finishes and plates, and the fire sprinkler system ({{inv_sprinklers}}): sprinklers need enough water flow and pressure, and without city water a tank and fire pump, a new septic system or a strict county can double that line, so get local quotes. In the country there is usually no sewer, so you need a septic system sized for your guest count; ask your county health department and an engineer. These are startup items, not extras: if your budget does not include them, something is missing.
80: Rain does not cancel a wedding, but it changes it, which is why the rain plan is part of the venue from day one. With the renovated hall ({{inv_reforma}}) and the ceremony site with a pergola and tent platform ({{inv_ceremonia}}) you can move the ceremony, the cocktail hour or the reception indoors without refunding anything. Set the criterion in writing, for example the forecast two days before, and put it in the couple’s contract so nobody is upset on the day. Well-kept grounds are part of what you sell: the initial landscaping is {{inv_jardin}}, utilities run {{suministros_mes}} a month and insurance {{seguros_anual}} a year. And one rule with no exceptions: when your fire marshal or county declares dry or high fire-danger conditions, no open flame, sparklers or grills, even if the couple asks. Check what your county and fire marshal allow.
81: Noise is what puts the most permits at risk. Your county ordinance and the conditions of your CUP set the limits and the music curfew, and the strictest rule wins. That is why it makes sense to install a decibel meter, hold the last dance indoors and point the speakers away from your neighbors. There is another issue that does not appear in the brochures: if the venue is served by its own well, a well that serves your guests may count as a public water system. Ask your state drinking water program, and plan for testing and a permit before the first event, with a written protocol. For anything else your county or state adds, check there. If you play recorded music, you also need the ASCAP, BMI and SESAC licenses that apply to venues.
82: The relationship with the caterer is written in the contract and practiced at every event. Agree on the tasting with the couple, the handling of food allergens and the schedule. Require that the caterer holds its own health permit for the kitchen it uses, its own liquor license or catering permit, liquor liability and general liability insurance with the venue named as additional insured. The venue does not sell or serve alcohol: the caterer does, under its own license. The caterer gives the couple written allergen information on the major food allergens as defined by federal law and your state or local rules. Reserve the right to review the food and beverage sales at your venue, with a monthly statement and an audit right, so the caterer commission is verifiable. The exclusive caterer agreement in this kit is a template, not legal advice: have an attorney review it.
85: The in-house team is short, because there are no servers or cooks: the caterer provides them. You are the manager, and the example pays you {{sueldo_titular}} a month: draw the rest from profit. Next to you there is a venue coordinator, a seasonal W-2 employee who handles tours, deadlines and the event day. There is also a facilities and grounds person, event attendants (seasonal part-time W-2 employees) for setup, parking and load-out, a part-time weekend sales person who sells dates and looks after the wedding planners, and a part-time housekeeping person. In total that is {{plantilla_puestos}} people.
86: That staff equals {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents and costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, or {{personal_pct}} of sales, including employer payroll taxes of {{cargas_pct}}. It is the biggest expense of the business, ahead of the rent ({{ocupacion_anual}} a year), so it is worth measuring well. Hours coverage is {{cobertura_horas}}, with {{personas_evento}} venue staff per event on average, not counting the caterer. If coverage falls short, you will feel it on a long setup Saturday; if there is a lot of slack, you pay for empty hours. Review it whenever you change the number of events or their size.
87: The venue coordinator and the event attendants are seasonal W-2 employees: put the offer in writing and rehire them in writing each season. They are employees, not contractors: never staff your setup crew with 1099 contractors who invoice you. If you set the schedule and direct the work, the law treats them as employees, and misclassification is a risk in an audit. Pay overtime where the Fair Labor Standards Act and your state require it, and ask your CPA how seasonal layoffs affect your state unemployment insurance. Events concentrate in the busy months; adjust the hiring dates to the calendar of dates sold and not the other way around.
88: As a wage reference, use the federal minimum wage, {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time schedule, and the higher of that and your state or local minimum. Enter your own in the "0. Assumptions" tab. Confirm your state’s rules with your state labor department before you sign the first contract. Keep time records: the Fair Labor Standards Act expects you to track the hours worked by each non-exempt employee, every day, above all on the long setup and load-out Saturdays. The plan uses a {{horas_semana}}-hour full-time week, the overtime threshold under federal law; some states add daily overtime rules.
89: On event day two teams work in the same house, and you have to decide who gives the orders. The rule is simple: your venue coordinator is the only point of contact for the couple and the caterer, and the caterer’s event captain leads its servers. Before every event, a short meeting with the hour-by-hour timeline, the rain plan and who cleans what avoids almost every misunderstanding. On the busiest weekends, around June and September, decide from the start who covers the extra hands, whether an extra attendant or support from the caterer. Improvising on the Saturday itself ends in rushing, setup mistakes and a worn-out team in the middle of the season.
90: Train the team before the first season: workplace safety, first aid and CPR, and evacuation. At a venue with a garden, a tent and children running around, knowing what to do about a fall, heat stroke or a fire alarm is part of the service. Practice an evacuation with the exit plan and the meeting point, and follow the occupant load and egress your fire marshal sets. The caterer trains its own staff in allergens, temperatures, food handling and responsible alcohol service, and shows proof in writing: ask for it in the contract.
93: To open you need {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} of startup costs (the build-out, the lease security deposit of {{inv_fianza}} and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent before opening, {{inv_renta_previa}}) plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The build-out includes {{inv_imprevistos}} of contingency, calculated as {{imprevistos_obra_pct}} of the build-out items. The cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. Financing is {{fondos_propios}} of owner’s equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed) and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection (often around 10% for SBA start-ups; many want 20-30%): ask your lender what it requires.
94: The three-year P&L projects sales of {{ventas_a1}}, {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}. Year 1 counts the full {{dias}} events, and you should read that carefully: it is only possible if the first season is sold during permitting and build-out with holds contingent on the permits, which become firm when you obtain them, because weddings are booked 12-18 months ahead. With that assumption the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, labor costs {{personal_a1}} and rent {{ocupacion_anual}} ({{ocupacion_pct}} of sales). EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}} ({{ebitda_pct_a1}}), after {{amortizacion_anual}} of depreciation and {{intereses_a1}} of interest the pre-tax profit is {{resultado_antes_impuestos_a1}}, and at an effective tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}} the net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} in year 1 and {{margen_neto_a3}} in year 3. Growth in years 2 and 3 is counted in equivalent events: {{eventos_equivalentes_a2}} in the second year ({{crecimiento_a2}}) and {{eventos_equivalentes_a3}} in the third ({{crecimiento_a3}}), at the same revenue per guest. In the Excel what grows is the average size of the event, from {{clientes_dia}} to {{clientes_a2}} and {{clientes_a3}} guests.
95: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year of the average size ({{clientes_dia}} guests), or {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} guests per event if you keep the {{dias}} events, with revenue of {{equilibrio_ventas}}. Cash break-even, which includes the loan payments and leaves depreciation out, is {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events in year 1, or {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} guests per event, with revenue of {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}}, and leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}}. In years 2 and 3 the margin is {{holgura_caja_a2}} and {{holgura_caja_a3}}. The real risk is occupancy: below {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events of the average size in year 1 there is no cash, so every date you do not sell shows.
96: The cash flow numbers its months from 1 to 12, and Month 1 is March. The ramp-up starts well below full pace and reaches full speed in 12 months, because weddings are booked 12-18 months ahead and the first season is booked before opening, contingent on the permits. The ramp-up does not remove sales from the year: it only shifts them toward the end, the way bookings arrive at a new venue. The lowest balance of the year, {{saldo_minimo}}, is in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, and the first spring is carried by the working capital, while the first winter is carried by the cash the season leaves. Retainers received early are not modeled, so your actual cash will be somewhat better. That is why pre-selling dates is the most profitable task of the first months.
97: The lowest DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, with {{dscr_a2}} in the second year and {{dscr_a3}} in the third: the business covers its debt, and your lender will want to see your pre-sold dates. A lender typically looks for a DSCR around {{dscr_objetivo}} or higher, against the workbook limit of {{dscr_limite}}. On payback: {{payback}}; that explains why the lease has to be long, with extension options: the build-out is depreciated over {{vida_obra}} years, so a short lease would sink the numbers. The example applies a sales tax rate of {{sales_tax}} to venue rental and services and none to the caterer commission; confirm how your state treats each.
98: The pessimistic scenario of the Excel is a first season that does not sell: {{pesimista_dias}} events of {{pesimista_clientes}} guests at {{pesimista_ticket}} per guest give sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}, with closing cash of {{pesimista_caja}} at the end of year 1. If you cannot book dates, contingent on the permits, during permitting and build-out, compare your case with this one. In the optimistic scenario, {{optimista_dias}} events of {{optimista_clientes}} guests at {{optimista_ticket}} leave sales of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}.
99: There are two reasoned alternatives, without Excel. With in-house catering the venue also bills the menu and the bar: sales multiply, but so do the investment, the kitchen crew and the food safety responsibility. It is a path for restaurant people, and the Catering Business Plan Kit covers it. With rental only, without the commission, the venue would sell {{ventas_espacio_a1}} instead of {{ventas_a1}}, which leaves little cushion over the cash break-even revenue of {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}}; check it in the Excel by setting the venue rental & services share to 100% and lowering the revenue per guest by the commission's share. That is why the case carries the caterer commission. Buying the property with an SBA 504 loan is a third route to discuss with your lender and your CPA; the workbook does not model it.
102: The first thing that decides this business is not the market, but the land. In a zone where the local code already allows the use, you may only need the building permit and the certificate of occupancy. On rural land, where most barn venues are, you typically need zoning approval first: a conditional (special) use permit from your county, often with a public hearing and conditions such as a cap on events, hours, traffic and noise. Check with your county planning office; the rules vary by state and county. Do not confirm firm dates without the permits: before you have them, take only fully refundable holds contingent on them. Make the lease contingent on CUP approval, so it only starts if you get the zoning approval and the certificate of occupancy. Because the build-out is on land you do not own, negotiate a lease whose term, counting extension options that only you can exercise, is at least the loan term (SBA lenders typically require this; confirm with your lender), plus a purchase option or right of first refusal, the owner’s consent to the build-out and to using the lease as collateral, and a tenant improvement (TI) allowance. Form an LLC with an EIN and ask your state and county which licenses and sales tax permit you need.
103: Converting a barn into a hall for guests is a change of occupancy to assembly use (Group A-2), which requires a building permit and a certificate of occupancy. Whether you need fire sprinklers depends on the International Building Code as adopted by your state or county, usually above an occupant load or fire-area threshold; editions and local amendments vary, so ask the building official and the fire marshal in writing. The fire marshal sets and posts the occupant load, and a tent has its own permit. Do not assume that a permit alone is enough: it is one piece. Sprinklers with a tank and fire pump, or a new septic system, can double the line in your budget, so get local quotes before you sign the lease.
104: The Americans with Disabilities Act (Title III) treats a venue that is open to the public as a public accommodation, with accessible routes, restrooms and parking. Do not assume an old building is exempt: ask your architect and your attorney what applies to your property. Water and sanitation matter in the country: a commercial septic system must be sized for your guest count, so ask your county health department and an engineer for the calculation. If a well serves your guests, it may count as a public water system: under the federal definition (40 CFR 141.2), one that regularly serves an average of at least 25 people a day at least 60 days a year. Ask your state drinking water program whether yours does, and what testing and permit you need before the first event.
105: On alcohol, the venue does not sell it. The exclusive caterer, or a licensed bartending service, serves it under its own liquor license or catering permit, with its own liquor liability coverage and the venue as additional insured. If couples bring their own alcohol, do it only with a licensed bartender and host liquor liability coverage from the client. Some states regulate venues that host events with alcohol, so ask your state alcohol beverage control agency what applies to you. Whoever serves checks IDs and never serves minors or guests who are visibly intoxicated. Do not tell clients the venue has a liquor license, and do not advertise an open bar as a venue service.
106: Sales tax depends on the state: some states tax the venue rental fee and others do not, sometimes only when it is billed together with catering, and the caterer commission is usually a business-to-business fee. The workbook applies {{sales_tax}} to venue rental and services and zero to the commission as an example only: ask your state’s department of revenue and your CPA. If you play music, the venue needs the ASCAP, BMI and SESAC licenses that apply. Noise is governed by your county ordinance and the conditions of your CUP, such as the curfew and the decibel limit, and you should check them before you promise a time for the end of the party.
107: For insurance, plan general liability, property, umbrella, host liquor liability and workers’ comp: the example uses {{seguros_anual}} a year as a Kit estimate, so get quotes from an agent who insures venues. Ask every outside vendor for a COI naming the venue as additional insured. In the contract, the retainer is applied to the price, the cancellation tiers are a reasonable estimate of the venue’s loss, not a penalty, with a rebooking credit, and an attorney in your state should review them; the cancellation table decides what is kept. If you sign couples at bridal shows or off-site, ask your attorney whether the FTC Cooling-Off Rule or your state’s home-solicitation law applies; many venues give a short cancellation window for show-floor signings anyway. For staff: seasonal W-2 employees, Form I-9, the Fair Labor Standards Act and your state minimum wage (the federal floor is $7.25 an hour, per the U.S. Department of Labor).
108: The venue only hosts the ceremony. The marriage license is issued by the county clerk, and who may officiate is regulated by each state, so check with your county clerk and have couples confirm it with the officiant. Everything else, check with your county, your state or your attorney: what is not here we do not assert. A note for the UK edition: a change of use for a wedding venue needs planning permission from your council; civil ceremonies need approved premises status (check with your council); VAT on venue hire is a question for your accountant; alcohol needs a premises licence and a personal licence; and you need a fire risk assessment under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005.
111: The conclusion is that a wedding and event venue of this size is viable, but it demands method and selling the dates on time. With {{dias}} events, year 1 leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} and a margin of safety over cash break-even of {{holgura_caja_pct}}; in years 2 and 3 the margin is {{holgura_caja_a2}} and {{holgura_caja_a3}}. The lowest DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, the lowest cash balance of {{saldo_minimo}} arrives in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}} and payback is {{payback}}. It is a business of patience, not of quick profit. If you compare it with other plans, notice that here the biggest risk is not the cost, but occupancy.
112: The first risk is the permit. With hearings and timelines that can run from 6 to 12 months or more, a venue without zoning approval cannot hold anything. You reduce it with a call to the county planning office before you sign, the lease contingent on CUP approval and the rule of not confirming dates without the permits (before you have them, only holds with a full refund). The second is occupancy: below {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events of the average size in year 1 there is no cash. You reduce it by pre-selling dates, contingent on the permits, during permitting and build-out, with agreements with wedding planners and venue marketplaces, which bring {{intermediarios_pct}} of sales at a {{comision_intermediarios_pct}} commission, and a calendar that does not depend only on weddings: corporate events, private celebrations and micro weddings.
113: The third is depending on the caterer. If there is only one and it leaves, you have no menu. Keep a preferred vendor list as a backup, sign a contract with a term, an auditable caterer commission and exit conditions, and remember that the commission is an assumption: negotiate it, because every point matters. The fourth is rain, which is solved with the hall and the tent. The fifth is noise and the neighbors: decibel meter, last dance indoors and speakers pointed away from the houses. One serious complaint can cost you the permit, so talk to your neighbors before the first event, not after.
114: The sixth risk is buying the property: it is often a seven-figure investment that this plan does not need; if you want to explore it, ask your lender about an SBA 504 loan. Lease a property with the buildings already built. The seventh is leasing it for too short a time: depreciating the build-out over a short lease sinks the numbers, which is why the lease needs extension options that bring it at least to the loan term, with reduced rent during the build-out and the owner’s consent to the improvements. The eighth is living only on peak Saturdays, with rent and staff flat all year: the busy season is concentrated, and the winter eats the cash of the season if there are no corporate events and private celebrations to fill it.
115: The ninth is thin insurance: ask for general liability, host liquor liability, workers’ comp and property coverage, require the caterer’s liability and liquor liability, and check the amounts with your insurance agent. The tenth is misclassifying the setup and parking crew as contractors: seasonal W-2 employees, always. And there is a plan B if the model does not convince you: the reasoned alternatives in section 2, in-house catering for people who are already restaurateurs, and rental only, which gives up the commission. None replaces the golden rule of this plan: not one dollar of build-out before you have the permit in hand.
116: The action plan for the first 90 days has three stretches. In weeks 1-4 you form the LLC, negotiate the lease with its contingency on CUP approval and call the county planning office. In weeks 5-8 you hire the architect and code consultant, apply for the conditional use permit and choose the exclusive caterer. In weeks 9-13 you sign the caterer agreement and work on the brand, the website, the photography, the first tours and the pre-sale of dates, always contingent on the permits. The checklist that comes with the plan has 84 tasks in six phases: 12 in Phase 1 - Business Setup, 16 in Phase 2 - Zoning & Permits, 15 in Phase 3 - Build-Out & Equipment, 13 in Phase 4 - Staff & Caterer, 14 in Phase 5 - Brand & Bookings and 14 in Phase 6 - Season & Events. Mark each task as you close it.
117: The next step is to complete the Excel with your own numbers: your real rent, your negotiated caterer commission, your event mix, your loan and your build-out calendar. Change only the green cells; this document reflects the numbers of the case, and yours are calculated by the workbook. Before you spend a dollar, ask your county what zoning approval your property needs, and do not sign the lease without the contingency on CUP approval. If the numbers still work after that, you will have a business with a base. If they do not, you will have lost an afternoon and not a fortune.
